keyVerseText: And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מַסָּע (maççâʻ) derives from the root נָסַע (nâçaʻ), which primarily means to pull up or set out on a journey. This root sense of projecting forward or setting out adds a dynamic dimension to the word מַסָּע, suggesting something that is sent forth or brought out, whether it be a physical object like a missile or a quarry stone extracted from its place. Thus, beyond the common English glosses such as "dart" or "quarry," the root implies an action of moving or projecting outward, emphasizing the process of bringing something forth from its original position.
usageInScripture: The word מַסָּע appears only twice in Scripture, demonstrating a dual usage that reflects its range of meaning. In 1 Kings 6:7, it refers to stones prepared at the quarry before being brought to the temple site, highlighting the idea of something extracted and made ready. In Job 41:18, the word is used in the sense of a missile or dart, emphasizing a sharp, projecting weapon. This variation between a static quarry and a dynamic missile reveals the core semantic field of objects that are brought forth or projected, whether by human craftsmanship or force.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַסָּע in its original semantic range enriches our appreciation of God's providence and the careful preparation involved in His works. The quarrying of stones before building the temple reflects God's order and forethought in the establishment of His dwelling place among His people. Simultaneously, the image of a dart or missile evokes the power and precision of divine judgment or protection. For the Christian faith, this word reminds us that God's purposes are both deliberate and active—He prepares and projects His will in the world with intentionality and strength, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the cornerstone and defender of His people.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 6:7, the phrase "stone made ready before it was brought thither" uses מַסָּע to convey that the stones were quarried and shaped off-site, ensuring that no noise of tools was heard during the temple's construction. This emphasizes the meticulous preparation and holiness surrounding the temple's building process, symbolizing how God's work is done with careful order and reverence. The word מַסָּע here highlights not just the physical act of quarrying but the spiritual significance of being set apart and made ready for God's purposes.
